Cheyenne and its historic districts

Cheyenne is Wyoming's capital and the seat of Laramie County, tucked into the state's far southeast corner. It stands at about 6,086 feet on Crow Creek and Dry Creek and covers a little over 32 square miles. The July 2025 estimate counted 66,507 residents. Two interstates meet southwest of town: I-25 runs north to south, I-80 east to west, and I-180 loops through the city along US 85. Cheyenne Regional Airport has daily nonstop United Express flights to Denver, and the Cheyenne Transit Program runs local buses.

Government, transportation, the military and a growing technology sector carry the economy. State offices, Union Pacific and BNSF rail yards, and F.E. Warren Air Force Base are long-standing anchors, and Microsoft, Meta, Magpul, Searing Industries and Eagle Claw are major employers. Cheyenne Regional, the local hospital, reports more than 2,000 employees. Sellers who work for the base or a large employer may need to move on a short timeline after a transfer or job change.

Five historic districts add a layer of review for homes inside them:

  • Downtown Cheyenne Historic District
  • Lakeview Historic District
  • Rainsford Historic District
  • Capitol North Historic District
  • South Side Historic District

Owning in one of them? Call Planning and Development about the rules before paying for repairs.

Hail and weather damage

Cheyenne is cold and semiarid, with strong summer thunderstorms, and hail does the most harm to a roof. The National Weather Service counts more than 6 days a year with severe hail of an inch or larger nearby, with June the busiest month and July next. Quarter-size hail is the most common report. It can fall anywhere from March into October, mostly late in the afternoon.

  • Annual precipitation is about 15.9 inches, mostly from May through August.
  • Seasonal snowfall averages about 60 inches, with March and April the snowiest months.
  • Lows reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit on roughly nine mornings a year.

Shingles, gutters, siding and furnace age get close attention from buyers and inspectors. Visible hail bruising on a roof can cut an offer or stall a financed sale. Someone paying cash for the house as is will not make you fix it first.

Is flood risk a concern?

Flood risk is a real topic because of the flash flood of August 1, 1985. The National Weather Service recorded 6.06 inches of rain in about three hours, 12 deaths, 70 injuries and more than $61 million in damage. A FEMA report afterward called for better stormwater and floodplain management, and the city put new drainage plans and retention projects in place in the late 1980s.

Today the city's Engineering Services Department keeps flood insurance rate maps and base flood elevations. Find it at 2101 O'Neil Ave., Room 206, or call (307) 637-6268. If your home is near Crow Creek or Dry Creek, check the map before you list. Lenders can insist on flood insurance, and learning that late can cost you days.

Permits and code rules before a sale

Cheyenne requires a permit for many repairs sellers consider, from reroofing, decks and garages to water heaters and electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Plan for a review of up to 10 business days, with fees tied to project value.

Some smaller jobs are exempt. A detached shed under 200 square feet needs no permit, and flatwork such as a concrete patio generally does not, unless it is in the city right-of-way. Fences over 6 feet need a permit, and the city limits fences to 4 feet in front of the house.

  • Carports over 200 square feet, or attached to another structure, need a permit.
  • Zoning violations can carry fines of $100 per day.
  • Structures built in a setback may have to be removed.

Short-term rentals are treated like other residential uses, so there is no separate registration, but each rental must hold the approvals it needs. If you have an unpermitted deck, shed or carport, call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 before a buyer finds it in an inspection.

Laramie County tax due dates

The Laramie County Treasurer, at 309 W. 20th Street in Cheyenne, collects tax that is billed in two parts.

PaymentPayable byIf unpaid
First halfNovember 10Paying the whole bill by December 31 waives interest on this half
Second halfMay 10 of the following yearDelinquent, with 18 percent interest per year

A bill still unpaid on May 11 goes onto a delinquent list certified by the treasurer, and the county holds a lien that can lead to a tax sale.

Ownership is fixed as of January 1. A buyer or heir who recorded a deed later may find the notice under the old name, but the tax is still owed. Schedules go out from the assessor by the fourth Monday in April, and a written objection must be filed within 30 days of mailing. More on appeals is in our Wyoming property tax guide.

Closing and recording

A deed for a Cheyenne sale is recorded with the Laramie County Clerk, which cannot accept it until a sworn statement of the price and terms is filed. W.S. 34-1-142 makes that statement confidential, so the sale price does not become a public record.

Recording costs $12 for the first page and $3 for every page after, and documents with several legal descriptions carry an added $15.50 administrative fee. The office is at 309 W 20th St, Suite 1600, and takes e-recording through several vendors. The counter is open Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

Expect the title company to deduct any open tax from your check before it files the deed, which makes an early call to the treasurer worthwhile.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Cheyenne houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How does a cash sale work in Cheyenne?

In a cash sale no lender is involved, which removes the appraisal and the loan approval from the timeline. Describe the property to us, wait while we review it, then decide on the offer.

It often suits people dealing with one of these:

  • An inherited house that needs probate paperwork and cleanout
  • A hail-damaged roof or older systems that would fail a lender's inspection
  • A military or job move with a fixed date
  • Back taxes or a payment problem that is getting worse

The purchase is as is. You pay no commission or closing costs, and declining costs you nothing. Call or text (424) 435-2326 or use the form on this page to start.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can I sell my house in Cheyenne?

Often faster than listing, since there is no lender approval or appraisal to wait on. Title work, probate and your chosen date set the pace. Give us your deadline and we will plan around it.

Do I need to fix hail damage before selling in Cheyenne?

Not when the buyer pays cash and takes the house as is. On the open market, a hail-damaged roof often comes up in the inspection and can lower the offer or require repairs. Reroofing needs a City of Cheyenne permit.

Is my sale price public in Wyoming?

No. Filing a deed requires a sworn statement of consideration, and W.S. 34-1-142 keeps it confidential and out of the public record. The county uses it only for statistics.

When are property taxes due in Laramie County?

The two halves are payable by November 10 and May 10 of the next year. A full payment by December 31 waives first-half interest, and delinquent tax runs at 18 percent a year.

Who do I call about a permit or a flood map in Cheyenne?

Call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 for permits and Engineering Services at (307) 637-6268 for flood maps and base flood elevations. Planning and Development at (307) 637-6282 handles zoning, fences and setbacks.

Casper and the towns around it

Casper sits on the North Platte River in east-central Wyoming and is the seat of Natrona County. The city stands at roughly 5,100 feet and covers about 27 square miles. Interstate 25 is the main route in and out, US 20/26 passes near the airport on the west side, and Casper-Natrona County International Airport has United Express and Delta Connection service.

Oil built the city, with the first refinery in 1895 and a boom that ran from about 1910 into the mid-1920s. The Texaco refinery closed in 1982 and the Amoco refinery in 1991, and population fell from 51,016 in 1980 to 46,742 in 1990. Today Casper is a regional center for banking, commerce and energy, with healthcare, manufacturing and tourism alongside. A Sinclair refinery still operates in nearby Evansville. Energy and construction jobs are a big part of local work, so a slowdown can strain an owner's budget and push a sale decision.

Several smaller places touch the city limits, so a Casper mailing address can fall under a different government than you would guess:

  • Mills
  • Evansville
  • Bar Nunn
  • Unincorporated areas such as Allendale, Dempsey Acres and Red Buttes

Find out if your parcel is in the City of Casper or out in the county before you sell, because that settles who issues permits and who enforces nuisance rules.

What does Casper weather do to a house?

Winters are long, cold and dry, and summers are hot and mostly dry, so heating systems and roofs take the most wear. The normal January high is 35.2 degrees Fahrenheit and the normal July high is 89.0.

  • Annual snowfall averages about 71.8 inches.
  • Annual precipitation averages 12.22 inches.
  • Highs reach 90 degrees on about 38 days a year.
  • Lows drop to 0 degrees on about 15 nights a year.

Snow can be extreme. The storm of April 3 and 4, 2023 dropped 26.7 inches in a day and 37.4 inches over two days, both records. After a roof collapse at a commercial building, the Natrona County building official listed warning signs for owners: creaking, visible sagging, cracked or split wood members, cracks in walls and doors that pop open.

A buyer's inspector will find any of those signs in your roof, ceilings or walls. A buyer paying cash for the house as is will still see them, yet you will not have to fix them before closing.

Flash flood and burn scar risk

Parts of Casper can see flash flooding, especially downstream from the slopes of Casper Mountain. On July 29, 2013 a flash flood warning covered the east side of the city after heavy rain fell on a recent burn scar from the Sheep Herder Hill fire. Several homes along the Clear Fork of Muddy Creek were damaged, and water covered East Second Street between Wyoming Blvd. and Hat 6 Road. Much of that day's rain came in about 20 minutes.

If your home is on the east side or near a creek, check flood maps and ask your insurer about coverage before a buyer's lender does. Tell a buyer about any past water problem up front.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Casper house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Permits and code enforcement

Most projects in the City of Casper need a building permit. The city works from the 2021 International Codes, covering building, residential, fire, plumbing, mechanical and fuel gas. Amendments are in Title 15 of the municipal code.

Small jobs follow different rules. Sheds under 120 square feet skip the building permit. A fence not over 6 feet high needs a fence permit but not a building permit. Platforms and walkways up to 30 inches above grade skip the building permit, and taller decks probably do not.

The Code Enforcement Division handles nuisance complaints, and the usual ones are:

  • Weeds and overgrowth
  • Litter and accumulated junk
  • Junk vehicles
  • Dangerous buildings
  • Recreational vehicle parking

The city contacts the owner or tenant first and asks for a correction. If the problem stays, the case may go to Municipal Court. Residents file complaints through the Casper 311 online form.

Natrona County property tax dates

Wyoming bills property tax in two halves. Natrona County's main office is at 200 N Center, Casper, phone 307-235-9200, and an online portal asks for your bill number, tax year, last name and total tax bill.

PaymentPayable byWhat follows
First halfNovember 10Paying the full amount by December 31 avoids interest and penalty on this half
Second halfMay 10 of the following yearUnpaid taxes are delinquent on May 11, and the treasurer demands payment

The tax follows the property, so an unpaid bill can surface at closing. Check your balance before you sign a contract. Our Wyoming property tax guide explains the appeal process.

Deed, sale price and recording

A deed for a Casper sale must come with a sworn statement of the full price and terms, and under W.S. 34-1-142 the county clerk cannot record the deed until that statement is filed. Wyoming law keeps the statement confidential. It is not a public record, and the county may use it only for statistical sales-price ratios. Transfers such as foreclosure sales and certain gifts between family members are exempt from the price disclosure.

Ahead of closing, find out from the title company what paperwork it wants from you, and get your tax balance from the county treasurer. Bring a photo ID and the deed if you have it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Casper houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How does a cash sale work?

Cash means we buy your house with no lender in the picture, so no bank appraisal or loan approval stands in the way. You share a few details about the home, we review them, and you decide whether to accept.

We buy the house as is. You pay no commission and no closing costs, and turning down the offer costs you nothing. It can fit a house with an old roof, deferred repairs, a code enforcement notice, or an estate that needs to be settled.

The steps are short. You describe the house, including the roof, heating system and any notice from the city. We review the details and make an offer. Once you accept, a title company searches the deed, pays any lien or unpaid tax out of what you receive, and files the deed with the county clerk after the sworn price statement. The closing date is yours to pick within what the paperwork allows, which helps if you are settling an estate or relocating on a deadline.

Call or text (424) 435-2326, or fill out the form on this page.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Casper house with a code violation?

Yes. Someone paying cash can buy a house with open nuisance or permit issues, and we buy as is. If you list the home instead, expect buyers to ask about notices from the Code Enforcement Division and about any unpermitted work.

Do I need a permit to replace a deck or fence in Casper?

Usually yes for a fence, since a fence permit is required even when the fence is not over 6 feet high. A deck up to 30 inches above grade is exempt from the building permit, but a taller one likely needs it. Confirm with the Building / Inspection Division.

When are property taxes due in Natrona County?

One half is payable by November 10 and the other by May 10 the next year. Anything unpaid on May 11 is delinquent. You can pay through the Natrona County online portal.

Is my sale price public in Wyoming?

No. Wyoming keeps the sworn price statement that accompanies the deed confidential under W.S. 34-1-142, and foreclosure sales and some other transfers do not need one.

Does heavy snow damage matter when selling in Casper?

It can. Casper averages about 71.8 inches of snow a year, and the April 2023 storm set records. Inspectors look for sagging, cracks and roof wear, though a cash buyer taking the house as is will not ask for those repairs first.

Selling in Gillette?

Gillette and the city limits

Campbell County's seat is Gillette, a northeastern Wyoming city that counted 33,403 residents in 2020. The city grew outward in stages, and on January 1, 2018 it annexed the Antelope Valley-Crestview area, which pulled a large residential district inside city limits. Westover, Foothills and the Westover Road corridor all sit in the developed core.

The boundary decides which rulebook your house lives under. A home inside the city follows city zoning, city permits and city water and sewer rules. A home just outside falls under Campbell County instead. City planning staff say owners can petition to annex land that touches city limits, and extending services is generally at the owner's expense.

Few Gillette houses are very old, because most building followed energy development. If yours went up in a boom decade, find out how old the roof, furnace and water heater are before you list. Buyers will ask.

Coal, jobs and buyer demand

Local money comes from coal, oil and coalbed methane, and a big share of Wyoming's coal is mined in the Powder River Basin around town. A drop in mine jobs or coal prices can cool house demand. If you have to relocate quickly during a slow stretch, the buyer pool may be thin, and a cash sale with a set closing date can look better.

Roofs, hail and winter wear

Winters are cold, summers hot and dry, and hail is common enough to affect roof values. On May 26, 2010, a hail storm hit the Westover and Foothills subdivisions hardest, and the Gillette News-Record estimated the damage could top $46 million, including $28 million for roofs and gutters. Roof age and gutters get close attention from local buyers.

Repeated freezing and thawing punishes old windows, thin attic insulation and poor grading. Repair or at least note those problems before an inspector does, and negotiations stay calmer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Gillette house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Permits and zoning rules

Structural projects inside Gillette generally need a building permit plus a zoning permit, and work done without them can snag a sale. Building Inspection and Planning both review a garage or addition. Decks, sheds and retaining walls usually go through the same two permits. A shed under 200 square feet or a retaining wall under 4 feet tall needs only the zoning permit.

City rules that tend to surface at sale time:

  • Fences need a free zoning permit. Front-yard fences are limited to 4 feet and side and rear fences to 6 feet.
  • A single-family zone permits one residence per lot, which rules out a second dwelling.
  • Each home must have two paved parking spaces off the street.
  • A business run from a residential home requires a Home Occupation Permit through Code Compliance.

To check how a lot is zoned, phone Planning at (307) 686-5281. Building can be reached at (307) 686-5200 or gillette@gillettewy.gov, and the city's online portal handles permits and inspections. Own a converted garage, a deck built without a permit or a basement apartment? Find out early if it can be legalized, or expect buyers to knock money off.

Tax calendar and exemptions

Bills go out from the county treasurer on or before October 10, on the statewide schedule. If you pay the whole year by December 31, the first half never goes delinquent.

InstallmentDue dateDelinquent after
First halfSeptember 1November 10
Second halfMarch 1May 10

Late balances carry 18 percent annual interest, so get current terms from the Treasurer before closing.

Applications for 2027 exemptions are open to homeowners and seniors, and to anyone claiming a veteran's exemption, from October 1, 2026 through March 1, 2027. The Homeowner's Exemption takes 25 percent off taxable value on the first $1 million of fair market value when the house is your primary residence. Owners 65 or older with at least 25 years of Wyoming residential tax payments can claim the Long-term Homeowner's Exemption instead, at 50 percent on the first $3 million. A veteran's exemption cuts assessed value by $6,000, and that filing is due the fourth Monday in May.

The Treasurer's number is (307) 682-7268 and the Assessor's is (307) 682-7266. Selling mid-year? The title company can explain how the current bill is split at closing.

How a sale gets recorded

Deeds go to the Campbell County Clerk, who also maintains the grantor and grantee indexes. Wyoming Statute 18-3-402 has the clerk mark each instrument with the day, hour and minute of arrival, and that stamp is the record date. Nothing is recorded until the fee is in hand. Phone the Clerk at (307) 682-7285.

City planners tell buyers to read the title report for easements, pre-annexation agreements and deed restrictions. Pulling your plat and any recorded agreements ahead of listing saves a round of questions.

A house that came through an estate needs documents showing who may sign the deed. Get those in order well before closing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Gillette houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Papers to gather before you sell

A little preparation shortens the closing. Pull your recorded deed, the plat and any easement or annexation agreements from the Clerk. Collect permit records for garages, decks and additions, and note any work that was done without one. Ask the Treasurer for your current tax balance, and find your mortgage payoff statement if you have a loan. With those in a folder, the title company has less to chase and you can compare offers with confidence.

Selling with taxes or liens owed

Delinquent taxes, a lien or a late mortgage will not block a sale, though each adds a step. The title company pays those balances out of your proceeds, so it needs payoff figures. Ask the Treasurer for the tax number and collect your mortgage statement and any lien papers.

Mention these items to your buyer at the outset. Surprises found during title work are what usually delay a closing.

Cash sale or listing

Typical Gillette sellers are dealing with old roofs, put-off repairs, inherited houses or a job move. Cash fits when you would rather avoid showings, repairs and a drawn-out loan approval.

Our cash offers price the house in its current state. We weigh condition, location and the work ahead, then present a number you can take or leave. You owe nothing for asking, and we name no price until we have seen the property.

  • Listing on the market: wider exposure and often a better price, offset by commission, repairs, showings and waiting on a buyer's loan.
  • Cash sale: quicker and simpler, though usually below what a fully prepared listing would bring.

Whichever way you lean, put the net proceeds side by side first.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Gillette house if it needs a new roof?

Yes. Hail has hit many Gillette roofs, the May 26, 2010 storm over Westover and Foothills among them. A cash offer accounts for the roof's condition, so replacing it first is not required.

When are property taxes due in Campbell County?

September 1 for the first half and March 1 for the second. They turn delinquent after November 10 and May 10, though full payment by December 31 keeps the first half clear. The Treasurer at (307) 682-7268 can confirm what you owe.

Do I need a permit to sell a house with an unpermitted deck or garage in Gillette?

No permit is needed just to sell. Still, unpermitted decks, additions and garages can delay a deal or pull offers down. Ask Building at (307) 686-5200 whether the work can be permitted after the fact.

Where are deeds recorded for a Gillette home?

At the Campbell County Clerk's office, (307) 682-7285. The fee is due up front, and the arrival date and time are stamped on the deed.

Does the Wyoming homeowner exemption affect my sale?

It reduces taxable value for as long as the house is your primary residence, and it does not get in the way of selling. The title company can explain how tax is handled at closing.

Laramie at a glance

Albany County's seat is Laramie, with 31,407 residents and 13,554 households as of 2020. The town sits at about 7,165 feet on the Laramie River, where Interstate 80 meets U.S. 287, roughly 50 miles from Cheyenne.

Nearly 3,000 people work for the University of Wyoming, the city's biggest employer, and a median age of 27.2 makes Laramie young for the state. That means a lot of houses are rented out, and a good share of sellers are landlords instead of people living in the home. With one large institution anchoring jobs, a change there can move local housing demand.

Winter and your house

Laramie is high, dry and cold. Annual snowfall runs about 48 to 50 inches, and freezing temperatures are possible from September 14 through June 6. At that elevation, heating costs and the weight of snow on a roof are ordinary concerns for every owner.

The city building office publishes local design criteria such as snow loads, wind speeds, frost depth and seismic classification in its Bulletin #2. Buyers will ask how old the roof and furnace are and how well the attic is insulated, so know the answers.

Building permits and zoning

Most residential projects and repairs in Laramie need a building permit. The city enforces the 2024 International Building Code, adjusted locally by Laramie Municipal Code Chapter 15.24.

These jobs are exempt from permitting:

  • A one-story shed or playhouse under 200 square feet, if it meets setbacks.
  • A fence no taller than 7 feet, but only in back and side yards.
  • A retaining wall up to 4 feet tall, measured from the footing bottom.
  • A freestanding deck under 200 square feet, no higher than 30 inches off the ground, that does not serve the front door.
  • Painting, wallpapering and comparable finish work.

File through the Civic Access online portal and allow an estimated three weeks for plan review. Code Administration is at 406 Ivinson Avenue, phone 307-721-5271.

Zoning follows the Unified Development Code, which sets many districts and overlays, among them the Aquifer Protection Overlay and the Gateway Overlay. Planning prefers that owners reach out before buying, changing a use or dividing land. The Planning Division is at 320 E Grand Avenue, (307) 721-5207, or planning@cityoflaramie.org.

If you have a finished basement, an old addition or an unpermitted deck, ask Code Administration what compliance would take. Do that first, while you still control the story.

Property taxes in Albany County

The state, not the county, sets the schedule. Each year's first half comes due on or after September 1 and can be paid on or after November 10, while the second half is due on or after March 1 of the next year and payable on or after May 10. Settle the whole bill by December 31 and there is no interest or penalty.

HalfDue on or afterPayable on or after
FirstSeptember 1November 10
SecondMarch 1May 10

Interest on late balances runs 18 percent a year. Reach the Treasurer at 307-721-2502 or the Assessor at 307-721-2511. An online county portal lets you look up and pay a bill, and the courthouse is at 525 E Grand Avenue.

Homestead-type exemptions

A primary residence qualifies for the Homeowner's Exemption, which removes 25 percent of taxable value on the first $1 million of fair market value. Older owners get a second option, the Long-term Homeowner's Exemption: 50 percent on the first $3 million, for those 65 or over who have paid Wyoming residential property tax for at least 25 years. In tax year 2027 the owner must occupy the home eight months of the year or more, and the County Assessor reviews every application.

Selling partway through the year? Your title company will explain how the bill is prorated.

Recording the deed

Recording happens at the Albany County Clerk, 307-721-2541, which also keeps the indexes of grantors and grantees. Under Wyoming Statute 18-3-402 each instrument is time-stamped on arrival, and the filing date is the record date. No document is recorded until its fee has been paid.

Selling a Laramie rental

Because so many Laramie houses are rented, a rental sale comes up often. A landlord has the usual items, a deed, tax balance and payoff, plus a lease. Find out when the lease ends and whether the tenant will stay or leave, since that decides whether a buyer takes possession at closing.

Deferred maintenance is common in rentals, and cash buyers take the house in its current state. That spares you from fixing a roof or adding insulation just to list. Compare that convenience against what a repaired, listed house might bring, then decide.

What to have ready for a sale

A folder of documents shortens the road to closing. Pull together:

  • The recorded deed, plus easements and agreements on file.
  • Permit records, or a list of work done without permits.
  • The current tax balance, from the Treasurer.
  • A mortgage payoff statement, if you have a loan.
  • For a rental, the lease and the move-out date.

Tenants do not block a sale, but the lease sets the timing, so raise it at the outset and the closing date can be built around it.

From there the steps are simple. A buyer reviews the house, the title company checks the paperwork and any balances owed, and the deed is recorded with the Clerk once the fee is paid. Taxes, liens and a mortgage payoff come out of the proceeds at closing, which is why the figures above matter.

When does a cash sale help a Laramie seller?

Laramie owners often hold rentals with deferred upkeep, inherited houses, or homes that want roof or insulation work before a move. A cash sale suits anyone who prefers to skip repairs, showings and a loan contingency.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Laramie house as a rental with tenants in it?

Usually, once the lease terms and timing are reviewed. Share the lease and the date the tenant leaves, and we can plan around them.

When are Albany County property taxes due?

The first half is due September 1, payable by November 10, and the second is due March 1, payable by May 10. Pay it all by December 31 to avoid interest. Check your balance with the Treasurer, 307-721-2502.

Do I need a permit for work on my Laramie house before selling?

Mostly yes, except small sheds, low fences, short retaining walls and finish work. Phone Code Administration at 307-721-5271 before you start. Selling itself needs no permit, but unpermitted work can complicate the deal.

Where do I record a deed for a Laramie property?

Take it to the Albany County Clerk, 307-721-2541. The fee is paid first and the arrival time is stamped.

Does winter affect selling a house in Laramie?

It can. Snowfall averages 48 to 50 inches a year, and freezing weather can arrive in mid-September and last into early June. Plan inspections and closings around that.
